questions.text:
Thanks for doing this. I couldn't open her phone myself.
I did Grandma's taxes for seven years. Two years ago she told me she'd manage on her own, and I let her.
Start with the simple number.
How much money is left in her "Current Account"?

That can't be right. 😔
She had over sixty thousand saved two years ago, and she never bought anything but books and bird seed.
Somebody was in her ear at the end.
Who was she calling night after night in her last weeks?
questions.hint: Check the recent calls in Phone.

questions.text:
No Ruthie in this family, and none that I shook hands with at the funeral.
I'm her executor. If money was going somewhere regular, I need the figure.
What's the largest amount that left her account every month for the same payee?
questions.hint: Scroll through her Current Account in RevoBank.

questions.text:
Grandma did the crossword in pen right up to the end. She didn't need a place like that.
So the money was for somebody else's bed. 😤
Who was she paying for?
questions.hint: Search her Mail for the same place.

questions.text:
I've never heard that name in my life.
A stranger, and my grandmother's whole savings. People like this find widows who live alone. I've watched it happen to clients.
Since what year had Grandma known Ruth?
questions.hint: Look at the oldest pictures in Photos.

questions.text:
That's before my father started school. So not a stranger. 😳
Then why did nobody ever say her name? Every year Grandma went away with her 'bridge club' and came back sunburned and happy.
We all live in Maine, so that doesn't help me. Which town did she actually go to on those trips?
questions.hint: Look through her past trips in Airbnb.

questions.text:
So the others had somewhere else to sleep. I'm starting to understand. 🥲
But it doesn't explain the money. Grandma would argue with telemarketers for sport rather than hang up on them.
If she ever shut somebody out, it meant something.
Who did she cut off completely?
questions.hint: In Phone, go to Recents, tap ⋯ at the top right and open Blocked Contacts.

onboarding.text: I'm Theo Marchetti. I'm an accountant, and three weeks ago I became the executor of my grandmother's estate. I've been through her paperwork twice now. The numbers don't add up, and I can't make them.
onboarding.label: Theo

onboarding.text: Grandma Odile half raised me. The library every afternoon, a book in my hands before I could ride a bike. I did her taxes for seven years. I thought I knew every dollar she had.
onboarding.label: Theo & Odile

onboarding.text: Odile Marchetti, seventy-eight, a school librarian for thirty-one years. Sharp, stubborn, careful with money. She died in her sleep at home on Carleton Street, with her savings nearly gone and a lien on the house.
onboarding.label: Odile

onboarding.text: I think somebody got to her at the end. Somebody who knew she lived alone. I have her phone and I can't bring myself to open it. Go through it for me. Follow the money.
onboarding.label: Theo

msgs.text: Morning, Grandma. Your estimated payment is due next month. Want me to pull the numbers like usual?
That is kind of you. I'll manage my own books from here, dear. Seven years is a great deal to ask of anyone. Love, Grandma
It's no trouble. It's literally what I do.
I know it is. That is why I would like to do this one thing myself. Love, Grandma
Okay. The folder stays on my desk if you change your mind.
I'll know where to find it. Eat something green today.
The finches have found the new feeder. I counted eleven at once. Love, Grandma
Eleven finches. Impressive.
Finished the crossword in pen again, ten minutes before my tea went cold. Love, Grandma
Show-off.
Off to the coast tomorrow with the girls. I've packed the cards. One cottage by the water and the four of us. Love, Grandma
Have fun. Wear sunscreen.
I'm seventy-six, dear, not made of paper. Love, Grandma
Home. Sunburned on the left arm only. The tomatoes survived without me. Love, Grandma
A man called about an extended warranty for the Subaru. I kept him on the line for twenty minutes. I enjoyed him enormously. Love, Grandma
Twenty minutes??
He had a script. I let him get to the end of it. He very nearly cried.
You can just hang up, you know.
Where is the fun in that?
Still on for dinner tomorrow? I'll bring the pie.
Of course. Come at four, dear, and I'll do the bird. Love, Grandma
The scarf is wool, so do not put it in the dryer. Love, Grandma
Reminder, the 1099-R should be in your mailbox by now.
It's in the drawer, sorted and labelled. Don't fuss. Love, Grandma
Not fussing. Just checking.
Your card is in the mail. Don't open it until the day. Love, Grandma
Got it. Twenty-eight. The ten dollar bill is still in there, I'm not twelve.
You are twenty-eight and you will accept it. Love, Grandma
Tax season is finally dead. Come for dinner? I'll cook. Badly.
I'd love to, dear. I'm busy afternoons these days but evenings are yours. Love, Grandma
Sold thirty-eight tomato seedlings at the library plant sale. A woman haggled me down on a basil. Love, Grandma
Did you let her?
I did not.
Heat wave coming. Is the fan in the back room working?
The fan and I get along. Drink water, Theo. Love, Grandma
Haven't heard from you in a few days. You good?
I'm out most afternoons, dear, a standing engagement. I'm perfectly well. Love, Grandma
A standing engagement. Okay, mystery woman.
Off on the bridge club trip tomorrow, the four of us, back in three days. The coast, with the girls. Water the tomatoes if you pass by. Love, Grandma
Which part of the coast?
The wet part, dear. Love, Grandma
Watered the tomatoes. Two of them split. Is that bad?
Home. Splitting means too much water, so you did a splendid job. Love, Grandma
I'll bring the green beans if you do the turkey. Love, Grandma
Deal. I'll try not to burn it.
Cold snap. Furnace okay?
The furnace and I have an understanding. Love, Grandma
Your card went in the post this morning. There's a poem in it. Don't groan. Love, Grandma
Twenty-nine. You wrote a poem again.
Eleven lines. I cut it down for you. Love, Grandma
Stopped by around noon, you weren't home.
I was out. I am out a good deal these days, dear. Library, the pharmacy, the usual. Love, Grandma
Tomatoes are in. Come and see the garden before the slugs do. Love, Grandma
Coming this week. I'll bring the good coffee.
Call me when you get a chance. Nothing's wrong. Just want to hear your voice.
I have a call at half past seven most evenings, dear. Try me after eight and I'm all yours. Love, Grandma
The first ripe tomato of the year, and it is the size of my fist. Love, Grandma
Save me a slice.
Grandma, call me back when you see this.
I called three times. Please pick up.
I'm driving over.
I don't know who else to say this to. I'm sorry I wasn't there.
Found an envelope with my name on it. Hymns for the service, typed. Of course you typed them.
Pauline hugged me for a long time at the funeral. She didn't say a word.
The tomatoes are ripe. I picked them. I didn't know what else to do with them.
I'm the executor. I never wanted to say that sentence.
The numbers don't add up, Grandma. I'm not accusing you. I just need to understand.
Found the crossword books in the kitchen drawer. All in pen. Not one crossed out.
Many happy returns, Odile! Seventy-eight and still sharper than the rest of us.
Thank you, Margie. I intend to spend the day doing the crossword in pen and eating a slice of lemon cake without feeling the least bit sorry.
As you should. Lunch later this month, on me. Tell me when.
The twentieth would suit. The Greek place by the post office?
Done. Noon.
What a pleasure. I won't tell you what that spanakopita did to my digestion; I'll only say I regret nothing.
Ha. My lips are sealed.
Did you see the paper? They're finally tearing down the old gym at Back Cove.
I did. I stood at the kitchen window and felt thirty years younger and ancient at once. I hope they keep the bricks.
They never keep the bricks.
Margie, do you still have the pattern for the cabled hat? The shop is out of the wool I want and I need to see the yardage.
Somewhere in the cedar chest. I'll hunt for it. Give me a few days.
Found it! Will put it in the mail tomorrow; a photo would only come out blurry.
Mail is perfect. I don't trust photographs of patterns; the numbers always swim.
The hat pattern arrived. Margie, you are a treasure. I cast on last night.
Show me when it's done. Though you'll need no help; I've seen your cable work.
My knee is on strike again. The doctor says it's the weather. I say it's the stairs.
Both can be true. Do you have the cane I gave you? Use it. Vanity is a poor crutch.
You sound like my daughter.
Your daughter is a sensible woman.
Odile, did the mailman leave a parcel at mine for you? I think there's a box with your name on it.
Probably my bird seed order. I'll come across in a minute.
Door's open. The box is heavier than a toddler.
Forty pounds of sunflower seed will do that.
Forty pounds! The cardinals will be fat as Christmas turkeys.
They are already.
Went to the lake with the grandchildren. Sunburn on my nose. Don't say it.
I would never. I will only suggest aloe, kept in the refrigerator.
You would say it.
I would have thought it very loudly.
I thought of going to the library sale preview on July 10. Would you want to walk through with me? I'd value your eye.
I'm on the committee, so I'll be there from eight; come at nine and I'll hide the good mysteries for you.
Corruption! I love it.
Finished that mystery you lent me. The butler did it, of course.
Margaret! You've spoiled it for the next borrower.
I'm joking. It was the niece. I'll return it today.
Thank goodness. And tell me what you thought over tea afterward.
I saw you leave with an armful. I have no complaints; it's a sale.
Enough to last me through August. Thank you for the preview.
You are most welcome. Come by for tea soon; the tomatoes are coming in and I've more than I can eat.
I'll take you up on the tomatoes. Is tomorrow all right? Around half past four?
Half past four will do nicely. I'll have the kettle on.
Running a few minutes late, parking is a circus.
Take your time, dear. I'm shelling peas on the back step.
That was a lovely visit. Thank you for the compliments on the hat; I'll finish the second one soon.
It was the nicest afternoon I've had in weeks. Same time next month?
Same time next month. Put it in your calendar, I've put it in mine.
Already done, bossy. Goodnight, Odile.
Goodnight, Margie. Mind that knee on the stairs.
Yes, ma'am.
This is the St. Dominic's Parish Office. You are receiving parish text updates. Reply STOP at any time to opt out.
Thank you. I did sign up at the back of the church; please do keep them to the essentials.
Lenten soup supper on March 6 at 6:00 PM in the parish hall. All welcome; donations go to the food pantry.
Will there be a sign-up for bread? I make a decent oatmeal loaf.
Yes, Mrs. Marchetti! Bread is always needed. Could you bring a few loaves?
Three loaves, then. I'll bring them at 5:30 so the kitchen ladies can slice.
Wonderful, thank you.
The Holy Week schedule is posted in the bulletin and on the church door. Easter morning Masses are at 8:00 and 10:30 AM.
Thank you. Is Father Boucher hearing confessions on the morning before the Vigil, as he did last year?
Yes, 9 to 10 in the side chapel.
Good. I'll be there at nine.
The Altar Society needs volunteers to launder the linens for May. Would you be able to take a week?
I can take the second week of May. Do they want starch?
Light starch please. Thank you, Mrs. Marchetti.
Good morning. Is the May crowning still at 10 tomorrow? It isn't on my bulletin.
Sorry for the confusion. It's moved to 11:30 after the late Mass. The bulletin was printed before the change.
That's all right, I'll adjust. Does the children's choir still sing?
They do. They've been rehearsing every week.
Parish rummage sale June 13, 8 AM to 1 PM. Donations accepted at the hall through June 10.
I have several boxes of knitting patterns and some glassware; is that wanted?
Absolutely, patterns go quickly.
Then I'll drop them off in the morning. Who should I ask for?
Ask for Bernadette in the hall office.
St. Dominic's Parish Office: Reminder: Altar Guild meets this month on the 9th at 10 AM in the parish hall. Coffee provided.
I'll be there. Should I bring the linens list?
Yes, please. Thank you, Odile.
Dropped off, finally. Four boxes in the end. Bernadette promised to keep the glass wrapped.
Thank you so much! We received them.
Rummage sale volunteers: please arrive at 7:30 tomorrow for setup. Coffee provided.
I'm not on the list; I'll come by as a customer after lunch.
Customers welcome!
Bought a lovely cut-glass bowl and then discovered it was one of mine. I paid for it anyway; it was for a good cause.
That's the best kind of donation!
St. Dominic's Parish Office: The summer bulletin is available. Mass times have changed; see the schedule posted at the church door.
Understood. I'll pick one up at the church door.
Parish picnic July 11, 1:00 PM at the Payson Park pavilion. Please bring a dish to share; sign up in the narthex.
I'll bring the green bean casserole with the crunchy onions; everybody asks for it.
Noted!
St. Dominic's: Bake sale proceeds support the food pantry. Please drop baked goods at the hall by 9 AM.
I'll bring oatmeal cookies, a good many of them.
St. Dominic's Parish Office: The Altar Guild thanks you for polishing the candlesticks. Beautifully done.
A pleasure; the brass was in need of love.
God bless.
Is the picnic still on despite the clouds?
Yes, the pavilion is covered. Rain or shine.
A very pleasant afternoon. Father Boucher ate three helpings of the casserole; I counted.
Thank you for coming! Reminder: the parish office will be closed July 17 for the diocesan staff day.
Noted. I'll call the week after if I need anything.
Mrs. Marchetti, the bulletin deadline is noon tomorrow; do you have a notice for the book sale?
I do: "Friends of the Portland Library book sale, all proceeds to the children's reading room." I'll email it by this evening.
Reminder: You have an appointment with Dr. Anand Krishnan on April 22 at 10:30 AM. Reply C to confirm.
C
Thank you, Odile. Your appointment is confirmed. Please bring your medication list and your blood pressure log.
Thanks for visiting today. Your blood pressure was 138/82. Please continue your current dose and return in three months.
Thank you. I'll keep the log faithfully; I write it in the margin of the crossword.
The crossword margin is as good a place as any 🙂
Good morning. I wonder if I could have a copy of last month's visit notes for my files?
Of course; we'll have them waiting at the front desk.
Thank you.
Your lab results are available. All values within the expected range. No action needed.
That is a relief; thank you for letting me know.
Your prescription refill request has been sent to Casco Bay Pharmacy.
Thank you. I'll collect it tomorrow.
Dr. Krishnan's office: Your blood pressure follow-up is scheduled for June 17 at 9:30 AM. Please bring your home readings.
Thank you. I have my readings written in the little notebook; do you want the whole month?
The whole month is perfect. Please take your morning dose as usual.
Odile, this is Maggie from Dr. Krishnan's office. Dr. K would like you to log your blood pressure morning and evening for a week and send us the numbers.
Certainly. Is it a concern? I'd like to know.
Just a check, one reading was a touch high. Nothing alarming.
I'll text the numbers on the morning of the 17th, if that suits.
Perfect.
Morning readings for the week: 142/84, 138/80, 146/88, 140/82, 136/80, 144/86, 140/84. The evening was slightly lower each day.
Thank you, Odile. Dr. K says to continue the same dose and go easy on salty snacks. Easy on the cheese!
The cheese is a hardship, but I shall bear it.
Home now. Please thank the doctor for his patience; I do talk a great deal.
He enjoyed it. A reminder to schedule your next visit in three months.
I'll call tomorrow.
Dr. Krishnan's office: Lab results are in and look good. No changes to your medication.
That's a relief. Thank you for letting me know so quickly.
Our pleasure. Enjoy your summer.
And you. I'll keep walking.
Reminder: your next appointment is on July 21 at 10:30 AM.
Thank you, I have it in the calendar.
Reminder: you have an appointment with Dr. Krishnan on July 21 at 10:30 AM. Reply C to confirm or call to reschedule.
C
Confirmed. See you then.
Portland Public Library: your hold A Gentleman in Moscow (large print) is ready at the Circulation Desk.
Thank you, I'll collect it this afternoon.
Portland Public Library: The item you requested, 'The Secret Life of Bees' large print, is ready for pickup at the Circulation Desk. It will be held for 7 days.
Thank you; I'll collect it tomorrow morning.
Portland Public Library: Items due in 3 days: 'A Gentleman in Moscow', 'The Pruning Handbook'. Renew online or call us.
Could I renew both by phone? I don't trust the website.
Auto-reply: Please call the Circulation Desk during open hours to speak with a staff member.
Called and renewed; the young man was very patient with me. Thank you.
Reminder: items due in three days: A Gentleman in Moscow.
May I renew? I've finished it, but I'd like to look at the last chapter again.
Renewed for three more weeks.
Portland Public Library: Your hold on 'Braiding Sweetgrass' is available.
Wonderful. I'll come in tomorrow.
Portland Public Library: 1 item is due in 3 days: The Remains of the Day. Reply RENEW to extend.
RENEW
Renewed. Your item is now due in 3 weeks.
Your hold Olive Kitteridge (large print) is ready.
Thank you; I'll come by this week.
Reminder: Olive Kitteridge is waiting at the Circulation Desk. Holds are kept for seven days.
Thank you. I'll collect it.
Odile! The squirrels have defeated your feeder again. I saw one hanging upside down at dawn like a trapeze artist.
I know. I watched him through the kitchen window with my tea. I've bought a baffle; Walt is going to help me hang it.
Good luck. They're smarter than we are.
They have more time to think about it.
Trash day moved because of the holiday, so bins go out tonight, not tomorrow.
Thank you for the warning; I'd have been standing at the curb on my own like a fool.
Do you have a long ladder? Mine is in my brother's garage and my gutter is hanging by a thread.
I have a stepladder and an aluminum extension in the cellar. You're welcome to either, but not to climb it alone; I'd like you in one piece.
Ha! Tom is coming next week to do it properly.
Sensible. Take the ladder anyway for the small things.
Your peonies are showing off. I can see them from my porch.
They're the one vanity I allow myself. Cut some if you like; I'll never get through them all.
Are you sure?
Very. Take as many as you like. Put them in the blue jug if you've one.
Odile, are you going to the garden club plant swap? I have far too many hostas.
I'd forgotten it was this week. What time?
This weekend at ten at the church hall. Bring cuttings if you've got any.
I have spider plant babies and a geranium that refuses to die.
Those are the best kind.
I'll see you there, then.
Did your lights flicker just now? Mine did.
Twice. I've got the candle and the flashlight out.
Back on. Phew.
The clock on the stove is blinking twelve; it will be that way until I fiddle with it.
I came home with your geranium cutting and three more plants from someone I can't remember. The house is a jungle.
Mine came home with a fern the size of a toddler. Where am I to put it?
The bathroom. They like steam.
Of course. The bathroom it is; I've always wanted a jungle.
There's a coyote report in the neighborhood group. Keep an eye out when you take the compost out.
I have no cat, thank heaven, but I'll mind the compost bin. Thank you for telling me.
My grandson graduated today! Cap and gown, the whole thing. I cried through the whole ceremony.
Congratulations, Janet! You must be so proud. Where is he off to in the fall?
Orono, the engineering program. God help the roommate.
He'll be fine. Send my love to the family.
Lovely morning. Coffee on my porch if you're up for it.
I'm on my way out the door at ten, but I can spare half an hour at nine.
Perfect.
Thank you, that was nice. Your porch has the best light on the street.
Heat wave coming, they say. Have you got your fans out?
I have the one in the kitchen and the good will of the oak tree. I'll manage.
Don't be stubborn, drink water.
I am drinking so much water I could float a toy boat.
Odile! Did you see the paper this morning? The city's finally fixing the crosswalk on Danforth.
I did, and I cut it out. I have been writing letters about that crosswalk since the spring.
You get the credit, then.
I shall accept it graciously and say nothing to anyone.
Fireworks start soon. My grandkids are here and very loud, apologies in advance.
Don't apologize. Children are the sound of a street being alive.
Crossword, "Shakespearean forest." Starts with an A and I'm stuck.
ARDEN. Now I've given you the answer; do admit you knew.
I did NOT know. You are insufferable. Thank you.
My grandson graduated from the community college program! Welding, of all things.
Janet, how wonderful. A trade is a fine thing; they will always need someone who can fix what is broken.
That's what I told him. His mother wanted law school.
Mothers do. Tell him congratulations from me.
Fourth of July parade today, do you want to walk down together? I'll bring folding chairs.
I'd like that. I'll bring a hat; the sun on Congress Street is merciless.
And lemonade. I'll bring the lemonade.
Then we're well provisioned. Meet at the corner by the bakery.
Did you see the fireworks over the harbor? We watched from the porch.
I watched from the back step with a glass of lemonade. The cat next door was most unimpressed.
Cats have taste.
Strawberries from the farm stand, too many for me. Want a quart?
I'd love a quart. I'll make a small shortcake; come over for a piece.
Deal.
Janet, the recipe for your blueberry buckle: I've lost the card. Would you send it again?
Of course. Three cups flour, a cup of sugar, a stick of butter... I'll copy it out properly and mail it.
Mail is fine; I like the handwriting.
Heat's supposed to break tomorrow. I'm going to make a big batch of that cold cucumber soup. Want some?
I would love some. I will bring my own jar to carry it home in.
I'll leave it on the porch in the cooler if I'm out.
Soup retrieved. Exquisite. Dill, and what else? There is something I cannot place.
Buttermilk and a little mint from the pot by the door.
Mint! Of course.
Mailed. Also my grandson is visiting; he's become a vegetarian and eats like a rabbit.
Then give him some of my tomatoes. Rabbits know tomatoes.
I'll tell him.
Odile, there's a package on your step. Want me to bring it in?
Yes please, dear; it's probably the bird seed. Put it inside the screen door.
Done. It's heavy!
Forty pounds of black oil sunflower. The finches will be pleased.
Do you want to go to the farmer's market on the 11th? They'll have peaches.
I can't that morning, I've a committee matter; but bring me a peach and I'll pay you back.
Deal. A couple of peaches.
Did you get one of those scam calls about your car warranty? That's the fourth this week.
I get several a day. I enjoy them. I told the last one I drove a horse and he hung up on me.
😂 Odile, you're terrible.
I have made it a hobby. It is much better for the blood pressure than being angry.
Got you three peaches, soft as butter. I'll drop them on your porch tomorrow morning.
Kind of you. If I'm not at the door, I'll be out back potting.
Here! Left them in the cooler bag on your porch. Didn't want to disturb you.
Found the peaches. I've just eaten one over the sink, as one must. Thank you, Janet.
That's the only proper way. Talk soon.
Humid today. Don't overdo the garden.
I'll keep to the shade and the hose.
Good. Evening!
We should do the farmers' market soon, before the peaches are gone.
Yes, let's. Say, early next week? I will check my calendar and let you know this evening.
Hi Odile, it's Carol. Book club is at my house this month, starting at 7. We're discussing Olive Kitteridge. Wine or cider?
Hello Carol. I shall bring cider and the last of my shortbread. I finished the book in a weekend; I am afraid I was not very fond of Olive at first.
Same!! Then she gets under your skin.
That is what I told myself at page ninety.
Thank you for coming tonight. Everyone loved your shortbread.
Thank you for hosting. I shall be thinking about that argument over the ending all week.
March pick is Gilead. The library has six copies on hold for us.
I own a copy; I will lend it to Louise if she hasn't one.
She'll be thrilled.
Meeting is at your place this month, correct? I keep confusing the rotation.
It is mine, yes. Seven o'clock; the chairs are in the hall closet and I will put out the good teacups.
You're a saint.
Hardly. I simply refuse to be outdone by your cookies.
Home safe! Thank you for a lovely evening, and for letting us run over by an hour. Gilead brought up a lot.
It did. I confess I wept in the kitchen after you left.
❤️ Me too, in the car.
April: lighter, I promise. Cranford? Short chapters, tea, nobody dies (okay, a few do).
A few do, indeed; but so gently. I read it every ten years or so. Count me in.
May's host is Louise, but her kitchen is being redone. Can we squeeze into the library's community room?
I can ask at the Friends desk; I am there most mornings this week.
Would you? You're our fixer.
Done. The community room is ours on the evening in question; they ask only that we stack the chairs.
Obviously 😄
Reminder: club tonight at 7, community room. We're on Rebecca. Spoiler policy strictly enforced.
I shall be there with my pen. I have read it four times, so I am allowed one smug smile.
Last night was hilarious. Did you see Doris's face when we got to the housekeeper?
I did. I nearly had to leave the room.
Odile, the grandchildren are coming for the whole of July and I am already exhausted. Any advice?
Keep a jar of buttons and a bottle of bubbles. Children can spend an hour with either.
Buttons! I'd never have thought. You are a genius.
I'm a librarian. We know what keeps small people quiet.
Bless you.
June's choice is a free-for-all. Everyone bring one favorite short story. Mine's The Lottery, don't judge.
You are a morbid woman, Carol. I shall bring Eudora Welty.
Perfect.
The bubbles lasted ten minutes and the buttons ended up in the dog's water bowl.
Better the dog's bowl than their mouths.
Ha! True.
How is the hip, by the way?
Hip is hip. The new cane has a handle like a duck. The kids adore it.
A duck-headed cane! Send me a photograph, I must see it.
What time are we meeting again? I wrote it on the wrong day on my calendar!
Tonight at seven, your house. Bring your short story and an appetite.
Ugh, thank you!
Fun night. We take July off, right? Too hot.
Indeed. I propose we reconvene in August and I will pick something very long and very boring.
You would not.
No, I would not. Something with a ghost.
Odile, I have more zucchini than a person can face. Would you like some?
I would! Zucchini bread is on my mind. Is it too much trouble to drop off?
No trouble; I'll leave a bag on your step tomorrow morning.
You're a saint. I'll give you a loaf in return.
Left them by the door. There are rather a lot of them. Apologies in advance.
I've counted nine. I'll bake tonight and freeze three loaves.
A woman of foresight.
Odile, I've lost my reading glasses for the third time this week. They were on my head.
Mine hang on a cord round my neck, and I recommend it to everyone; it is the one sensible fashion of old age.
I'll order a cord. Beaded, I think.
Plain. Beads clack.
How is the loaf?
Delicious, if I say so myself. I put walnuts in. I'll bring yours around tomorrow.
Wonderful. I'll put the kettle on.
Odile, any thoughts for August? Louise wants a mystery.
Dorothy Sayers. Gaudy Night, if everyone can stand its length. Rainy evening reading.
Oh, I love that. Putting it on the schedule.
The loaf is on your porch, wrapped in a tea towel. The towel is a loan; I want it back.
Ha! I'll launder and return it. You're a tyrant about towels.
It was my mother's.
Then I'll return it with honors.
I tried to send you a picture of the duck but the phone refused. I'll show you in person.
Photographs and I are on difficult terms, dear. In person it is.
Tea next week?
Do you remember the name of the woman who ran the school fair years ago? Starts with a P.
Pinkham; Muriel Pinkham. She'd have run the Normandy invasion if you'd let her.
That's her. Thank you, my brain is a sieve.
Your brain is perfectly good; it's just too busy.
Towel is returned to your porch, with a small jar of my peach jam. Don't say I never gave you anything.
Odile, your recycling bin blew into my yard again. I've set it back by your gate.
Thank you, Helen. That wind was ferocious this morning. I will weight it with a brick.
Brick works. Pick an ugly one 😄
I have a very ugly one in the garden shed.
Seedlings! I have more Early Girls than I know what to do with. Want a half dozen for your back bed?
I would be delighted. Last year's yield was ridiculous; I was handing tomatoes to the mail carrier.
Ha! I'll bring them over when it warms up.
Helen, the seedlings are in. I put them against the south fence. Do you think frost is still a danger?
Cover them tonight to be safe. Old bedsheet.
I have the very sheet. Thank you.
Did you see the notice about street sweeping? They're coming tomorrow morning, so cars off the street by eight.
I had not seen it. I shall move the Subaru into the driveway this evening.
Perfect.
Good morning. Something has been at the bird feeder again; the pole is bent. Have you seen anything?
Squirrel, I'd bet. Mine got into the suet last week. Try Vaseline on the pole.
Vaseline! How undignified for the squirrel. I shall try it.
Report back.
Report: one squirrel, defeated, sliding down the pole like a child at a playground. I watched for twenty minutes.
😂 You're my hero.
Your casserole dish is still on my shelf. The one with the blue rim. I keep forgetting to walk it over.
Keep it a little longer; I will come by for it this week with a loaf of bread.
Deal. Banana bread?
Zucchini, if I can find a good one.
Odile, the reunion committee wants a list of retired staff from Back Cove. Do you still have the old directory?
I do, in the bottom drawer. It's from before I retired, so some of the addresses are dead and some of the people are too.
Oh, Odile 😂 Well, send what you can.
I'll type up the names tonight. My typing is slow but it is accurate.
Accuracy is all we've ever needed.
List is done; forty-one names. I've marked the ones I know have moved to Florida.
You're a wonder. Mrs. Larkin's gone to Florida, I know that much.
I put a star next to her. And Mr. Dube, who has gone to his daughter's in Vermont.
Perfect. Lunch after the meeting, my treat?
Only if I can have the soup and half a sandwich.
Helen, a package came to my door addressed to a Mr. Hollis at your house number. I have left it on your step.
Oh, thank you! That's my brother-in-law's fishing reels. He has them shipped here so his wife won't see.
My lips are sealed.
Did you hear the noise last night? Somebody's graduation party. Rattled my windows.
I slept through it; one advantage of being old and deaf in the left ear.
Lucky you.
The hydrangea is finally blooming. Come see before the rain.
I will come over with my camera this afternoon.
They are magnificent, Helen. The blue ones especially. I think it's all the coffee grounds.
Coffee grounds and a little rusty nail, my mother's trick.
I will try the nail.
Odile, book club is at my place on the 16th. Do you have the novel yet?
I've finished it. A bit too long, with a very satisfactory last chapter.
Don't spoil! I'm only on chapter nine.
I never spoil. I only hint, vigorously.
Reunion is set for the fall, at the school cafeteria. The new principal says we can use the library too.
How kind of her. I'll bring the old yearbooks if they let me.
They'd better. You'd be the main attraction.
I'd be the main nuisance, dear. Count me in.
Have you got the wine or shall I get it?
I'm bringing the cheese, and you've the wine. I don't touch wine before the evening; Frank used to tease me for it.
Wine, then. Red or white?
White. It's too warm for red.
Happy Fourth! Are you doing anything?
A quiet one; a visit to a friend, and then the cucumber sandwiches I always say I will stop making.
Never stop.
My new hearing aids have arrived. I can hear the refrigerator humming. It's a horror.
You'll adapt. A cousin of mine said the same, and by the end of a week she couldn't do without them.
I'll hold my tongue and my hearing.
Do you know a decent plumber? The upstairs faucet is dripping.
Beaulieu Plumbing, on Forest Avenue. They were honest with me.
Thank you, I'll call today.
Plumber came. Thirty minutes and a washer. $75. Honest indeed.
I'm glad. Honest people are worth their weight in gold.
Tomatoes coming in yet?
The first one turned this morning. I shall leave it on your step in a paper bag, like a ransom.
I'll pay in squash. 🍅
Reminder to bring the cheese for the 16th. Brie please.
Brie it shall be, and some crackers. And grapes.
Odile, I forgot to say, Maribel can't come this month. So it's a small group.
A small group is the best kind; we can sit around your table and argue properly.
You argue improperly and enjoy it.
I'll grant you that.
See you on the 16th. Goodnight!
Reminder from Friends of the Portland Library: the book club meets this month on the 15th at 10 AM in the Reading Room. This month's title is Gilead.
Thank you. I'll be there with the book and, I hope, some opinions.
We'd expect nothing less 🙂
Good morning! Coffee is on in the Reading Room. Please sign the sheet at the door.
On my way. I'm parked and walking in.
Thank you for a lively discussion. Next month's selection is The Remains of the Day. Copies are on the hold shelf.
I read it years ago; I shall read it again with more patience. Thank you for the reminder.
Odile, we are short one volunteer for the spring book sale sorting. Could you spare an afternoon?
I can give you the whole afternoon. Sorting is the one task I never tire of.
You're a lifesaver. Boxes arrive at the side door at one o'clock.
I'll have my reading glasses and a pencil.
Book club reminder: tomorrow, 10 AM, Reading Room. We are discussing The Remains of the Day.
Noted. I'll bring the lemon cookies.
Thank you all for coming. A few of you asked about the author's other novels; there's a list at the desk.
June selection: A Gentleman in Moscow. It's a long one, so start early. We meet on July 9 to finish it.
I've begun it already; the first chapters are delightful.
Annual appeal letters go out this month. Would you be willing to help stuff envelopes on the 17th?
Yes, certainly. I have a very good envelope tongue, as I'm told.
😂 Please bring your own pen!
Friends of the Portland Library: Reminder, the book sale sorting day is this weekend at 9 AM in the basement. Volunteers welcome!
I'll be there with my reading glasses and a box of rubber bands.
Wonderful! Sign-in sheet will be at the side door.
Friends of the Portland Library: Book club this month is 'The Remains of the Day'. Meeting on July 9 at 1 PM, Reading Room.
Will there be tea? Last month there was only that dreadful decaf.
We'll bring proper tea, we promise.
Then I shall bring lemon bars.
Thank you for stuffing envelopes today. We mailed over four hundred!
It was a pleasure; my fingers are sticky, but my heart is full.
Friends of the Portland Library: Thank you to all who helped with the sale! We raised $1,846 for the children's room.
That's marvelous. The children's room needs new beanbags; the old ones are held together with tape.
Noted for the next budget meeting!
Summer schedule: the book club will meet at the Congress Street branch while the Reading Room is painted.
Congress Street is easy for parking. Thank you for telling me.
Reminder: book club tomorrow at 10 AM. We are finishing A Gentleman in Moscow.
Friends of the Portland Library: Summer newsletter is out. Pick one up at the front desk or reply for a mailed copy.
I'll be there; I've finished, and I cried a little at the end, I admit.
Please mail mine. I like to read it with breakfast.
Don't spoil it for those still reading! 😄
Thank you for a wonderful discussion. The August selection is Olive Kitteridge.
Splendid. I'll put in my request for the large print copy.
Hold placed. It will be ready at the desk.
Also, the Friends dinner is next month; may we count you in?
Yes, count me in. I'll tell you if I need a ride; I'd rather drive myself.
Wonderful. Invitations go out soon.
Thank you for all you do.
It's a pleasure to have you with us.
Hi Odile! This is Lena's Hair Studio reminding you of your cut tomorrow at 10:30 AM. Reply C to confirm.
C. Thank you, Lena; I will be there with my hat on, as it is supposed to snow.
Ha, stay warm! See you then.
Thanks for coming in today, Odile. Your next visit is booked for March 18 at 10:30 AM.
A lovely cut as always. Please tell Dot the tip is in the envelope.
Reminder from Lena's Hair Studio: you're booked tomorrow at 10:30 AM. Reply C to confirm.
C. Will there be time to tidy my eyebrows too, or is that a separate charge?
Brows are $10 and take ten minutes. I'll pencil it in!
Please do.
Odile, so sorry, we're running ten minutes behind. Could you come at 10:40 instead?
Of course. I shall finish the crossword in the waiting chair.
Thanks for coming in! Your next appointment is booked for April 30 at 10:30 AM.
Lena, I have a small favor to ask. A friend of mine is turning eighty next month and I would like a gift certificate for a wash and set. May I pick one up on my next visit?
Absolutely! What amount?
Sixty dollars, please. In a nice envelope if you have one.
Will do. 💐
Reminder from Lena's Hair Studio: you're booked tomorrow at 10:30 AM. Reply C to confirm.
C
All set! The gift certificate is in your bag. Next visit is June 11 at 10:30 AM.
Thank you, dear. She will be thrilled. I left the tip with Dot.
Lena's Hair Studio: Hi Odile! Your trim is due. We have tomorrow at 11 or the day after at 3. Which works?
Tomorrow at 11, please.
Booked! See you then.
I'm running a few minutes late; Forest Avenue is behind a delivery truck. Please don't give my chair away.
No worries, we'll have the cape ready.
It was lovely to see you today! Pixie looks sharp. Leave us a review if you have a moment 💇
Thank you, dear. I don't do reviews, but I'll tell everyone at the library.
Reminder from Lena's Hair Studio: you're booked in two days at 10:30 AM. Reply C to confirm.
C
Heads up, Odile: there is water main work on Exchange Street, closed to cars until noon. Park on Market Street.
Thank you for the warning. I shall walk the last block; the exercise will do me good.
Great seeing you! Should I put you down for the same time in six weeks?
Yes please; and I will keep the pixie. I tried to talk myself into growing it out and failed.
Ha! It suits you. Booked for the end of July, I'll text you the exact date.
Lena's Hair Studio: Time for your next trim in about a month!
Put me down for after the holiday, please.
Done: the 9th at 11.
Hi Odile, it's Lena at the studio. We got a new shampoo line in and I wondered if you'd like to try the lavender one. No pressure!
Lavender is lovely; I shall try a small bottle. Is it very expensive?
$14 for the small one. I'll set one aside for you.
Wonderful. Put it on my account.
Reminder from Lena's Hair Studio: we will be closed the last week of July while Lena is on vacation. Your appointment has been moved to the first week of August.
That is perfectly fine. Does Lena go somewhere nice?
Her sister's place in Vermont. A lake and a lot of sitting around.
The best kind of holiday. Tell her I said to rest.
Will do! Take care, Odile.
One more thing: the hair clip left in my bag last time is not mine. Shall I bring it back?
Oh, that's Dot's! Keep it for now, she'll never miss it.
Very well. I shall return it in August.
Odile, did you see the notice about the parish rummage sale? They are short of volunteers for the book table.
I saw it. Of course they want me on the book table; I'll take the morning shift.
Wonderful. I'll put you down for nine until noon.
Nine is fine. Will you bring the cash box, or shall I?
I'll bring it. Father Luc says the proceeds go toward the boiler.
That boiler has eaten more of our money than the Sunday collection.
Don't let him hear you 😄
Odile, I have a loaf of the cranberry bread for you. Are you home this afternoon?
I'm at the store until four, then home. Come by whenever; the kettle is always on.
Perfect. I'll leave it on the step if you're out.
The bread is lovely, thank you. I had a slice with butter standing at the counter like a schoolgirl.
That's the only proper way to eat it.
Morning. Are you going to the diocese luncheon? I can drive if you'd rather not do the highway.
Thank you, dear, but I'll drive myself; I have an errand afterward and can't be held to anyone's schedule.
Fair enough. Save me a seat near the door, the room gets stuffy.
Near the door it is.
Did you hear what Father Luc said about the bake sale? I nearly dropped my fork.
I heard. Mrs. Dunphy will be insufferable for a month.
My daughter wants me to get one of those smart speakers. Do you have one?
I do not. I have a radio, a telephone and a perfectly good calendar on the wall. There is one in this phone too, but only because it nags me about my pills.
Good, I'll tell her you said no.
The lilacs at the church are going over already. Too warm too early.
Mine too. The tomatoes are pleased, however; I put them out last week and not one has sulked yet.
You and those tomatoes.
They're better company than most people.
Odile! Ma chère, I found the photograph of Maman's kitchen in Lewiston. Do you want a copy?
Oh, yes please. I'd love one; I'll scan it for the album so it doesn't fade.
I'll mail it tomorrow. Don't lose it in your piles of books 😉
My piles are very organized, thank you.
Of course they are. How is the garden?
The tomatoes have flowered. The squirrels have opinions about them, naturally.
Are you coming to the funeral lunch for Agnes Rowley? The family asked for a head count.
Yes, put me down. I'll bring a plate of those lemon squares.
Bless you. The Rowleys will be grateful.
Marguerite, would you remember the name of the man who did your gutters? Mine are sagging at the back corner.
It's Tom Gagnon. He's honest, which is rare.
Thank you; I have him in the phone already, I'd forgotten.
That's what the phone is for.
Tourtière recipe, the one Maman made at Christmas. Do you remember how much clove?
A scant teaspoon, I believe; she always said too much clove tastes like a dentist's office.
Ha! Yes, that's it exactly.
Write it on the card in ink this time.
Fireworks tomorrow night at the waterfront. Will you go?
I don't think so; the crowds are more than I can take now. I'll sit on the back step and listen to the neighbors.
I'll bring you a sparkler then.
The new priest's sermon was forty minutes long. Forty!
I timed it. Forty-three, if you count the announcements.
Photograph is in the mail. It's a bit creased at one corner, forgive me.
A crease is a sign it was loved. Thank you, Marguerite.
Heat coming this week. Drink water, Odile, and keep the curtains drawn.
Hi Odile, it's Sandy at Wool & Thistle. Your order of the moss green wool has arrived.
Wonderful. I'll come by this afternoon.
We close at six.
I'll be there by four.
I'm in the parking lot; the door is locked, is anyone there?
Sorry! Go around the side, I'm in the back with the new shipment.
Pattern update: the cabled hat pattern you wanted is in. Want me to hold a copy?
Yes, please hold it. It's for the fair table at church.
Held under your name.
Sandy, would you have size seven circular needles in the sixteen inch?
I do. I'll set them aside along with the stitch markers you liked.
Thank you. I'm a slow knitter now; my knuckles object.
Slow is fine. The hat will be just as warm.
Reminder: the Wool & Thistle summer sale begins today. Twenty percent off all cotton blends.
Cotton does nothing for me, but thank you.
Ha, I'll save you the good wool for fall.
Hi Odile, it's Sandy at Wool & Thistle. The merino you asked about came in, the moss green. Shall I set aside four skeins?
Yes, please; four skeins should be enough for a cardigan. I'll come tomorrow.
Perfect, I'll put it under the counter with your name on it.
Thank you. Will you have any needles in size seven?
Plenty. Bamboo or aluminum?
Bamboo; they're kinder to my knuckles.
Your yarn order shipped yesterday, should be with you in a few days.
Thank you. I do like a parcel.
The yarn arrived and it is lovely. Please add a skein of the oatmeal for the trim.
Will do. I'll put it in with the next shipment.
Odile, we're starting a weekly evening knit night next month, tea and biscuits. Want me to add you to the list?
I'd be glad of it. I do need an excuse to finish things.
Then we'll save you a chair by the window.
How lovely. Thank you, Sandy.
Odile, a customer asked about your cabled cardigan. She saw it at church and wants to commission one!
Commission! At my age I knit for pleasure, not payment. Tell her I'll give her the pattern if she buys the yarn here.
That's very generous. I'll tell her.
Oatmeal skein is in. Shall I hold or ship?
Hold it, please. I'll come by next week when my errands bring me past.
Great. We have fresh tea in the shop if you'd like a cup.
I'd like that very much.
Hi Odile, just a note: the shop is closed for inventory on the 20th. Back to normal after that.
Noted, thank you for the warning.
See you soon!
Casco Bay Pharmacy: Your prescription is ready for pickup. Store hours until 7 PM.
Thank you, I'll be there before noon.

Odile, it's Joanne Pelletier from Back Cove. Margie Doucette gave me your number, I hope that's all right.
Joanne! Of course it is. How lovely to hear from you; I believe it has been since the retirement tea for Mr. Hallett.
That's the one. I'm organizing a luncheon for the old Back Cove staff. Thought it was time, before we're all too decrepit.
Speak for yourself, dear. I'm perfectly sturdy. When and where?
Thinking May 16, noon, at the Village Cafe on Forest Ave. Does that suit?
That suits. I'll mark it on my calendar now. Is it a sit-down or a buffet?
Sit-down. Chicken or the haddock; I'll need your choice by the end of the month.
Haddock. I never trust chicken at a luncheon.
Ha! Haddock it is. Seventeen people so far.
Joanne, a thought: shall I bring the old yearbooks? I still have the ones from the nineties in the hall closet.
Oh would you? That would be the hit of the day. Heaven knows what we looked like.
Like women who had never heard of a hair dryer; but I'll bring them.
Reminder, haddock lady: the cafe wants the head count by tomorrow. Still a yes?
Still a yes. Should I bring anything else besides the books?
Just yourself. Oh, and do you have Lorraine Beck's address? Her card came back.
I do, in my address book at home; I'll text it this evening. She moved to Brunswick, to be near her daughter.
Here it is: 18 Maple Court, Brunswick. Tell her we'll save her a seat.
Perfect, thank you. Reprinting the invitation for her.
Joanne, is the luncheon still on for this weekend? I want to be sure I have the day right; my calendar says so.
It is. Noon sharp. Wear something warm, the cafe keeps the air conditioning like a meat locker.
Home safe. What a wonderful afternoon. I haven't laughed like that since the faculty talent show.
Wasn't it? Eleven of us said we should do it every spring.
Then we shall. You'll organize; I'll bring the yearbooks and nothing else.
Deal. Also someone took a snapshot of you with Dolores Winn, I'll have it printed and mailed.
Joanne, how did the hip appointment go? Margie said you were nervous.
Surgery is scheduled for the end of the month. They say a six week recovery. I'll be a very bored woman.
Then I'll send you books. What do you like these days? Still the cozy mysteries?
Still cozy mysteries. The ones with cats and bakeries; nothing with bodies in the first chapter.
I will pull a stack from the sale shelf at the library. Cats and bakeries it is.
Odile! The kids found a box of your old bookmarks in the closet, the laminated ones with the owls. Do you want them back?
Goodness, I'd forgotten. Keep them; they're for the children.
They're very popular. One boy cried when I ran out.
Then I'll laminate more. Send me a count of what you need.
Thirty, if it isn't too much trouble.
It's no trouble at all. I'll drop them by the front office.
Bookmarks arrived! The librarian's assistant squealed. Thank you thank you.
My pleasure; I enjoyed it. The owls are getting a bit cross-eyed, I'm afraid, from the cheap laminator.
They have personality.
That's one word for it.
Out of the hospital. Home since yesterday. The walker is the least dignified object I have ever owned.
Welcome home, dear. Are you being looked after? Shall I bring soup?
My sister is here until the end of the week. After that I'd love a visit.
I'll come on July 7 with soup and the cats-and-bakeries. Is minestrone all right?
Minestrone is perfect.
On my way over now, I'll be there in about twenty minutes. Please don't get up.
Door is open. I couldn't get up if I wanted to.
Home. Your garden looks lovely; those hydrangeas are showing off.
Thank you for the soup, and the books, and the company. I'm already on the second mystery. The baker did it.
School's out. I'm sleeping until noon every day for a week.
You've earned it. Sleep in; the children will be there in September.
Don't tell me who did it! I borrowed one of those myself and I'd like to be surprised.
Then I'll say nothing. Walker report: I made it to the mailbox and back. A triumph.
Did I leave my casserole dish at yours?
Second shelf. Come and get it before I start cooking in it.
Tomorrow after ten? I'll bring muffins.
Bring two extra. Walt has shoveled for me all winter and I still owe him.
Blueberry or bran?
Blueberry. Nobody has ever thanked anyone for bran.
Odile, my knee is acting up again. The doctor says it's the weather. I say it's the doctor.
Odile, do you still have that cable-knit pattern with the little acorn border? Mine went through the wash in a coat pocket.
Doctors are always sure it's the weather. Ice and a good book, that's my prescription.
I do; it's in the green binder. I'll copy it at the library and drop it in your mailbox.
I'm taking it. Tell me you're coming to the church supper.
You're a saint. I'll owe you a lemon loaf.
Make it the one with poppy seeds and we're square.
I'll bring the green beans. Do they still want them with the almonds?
They want them with the almonds and without the bacon, bless them.
Without the bacon is a crime, but I'll comply.
Did you see the forecast? Rain all week.
I did. The tomatoes will be drowning; I'm going to hold a vigil with an umbrella.
😂 You'd do it too.
Biscuit has decided that the vacuum cleaner is a personal enemy. He barked at it for an hour.
Dogs are very good judges of character. Give him a biscuit for his troubles.
That's his name, dear, he'd think you were mocking him 😄
Then I'll give him a carrot. Mind the stairs; you said your knee was complaining.
Happy Fourth! Watching fireworks from my window. I'm too old for the crowds.
Same. I'm on the back step with a glass of iced tea.
To the quiet life.
Knee is better, thank you. The doctor says walk more, so I walk to the mailbox and back, slowly.
Slow is still walking. Be careful of the loose brick by your gate.
Do you remember that casserole recipe from the school fair? The one with the breadcrumbs?
The tuna one? I have it on a card. I'll copy it out and mail it, as you won't trust a text.
You know me well.
It'll be in the post tomorrow.
Bayside Bird & Garden Supply: thanks for joining our text club! Spring seed order forms are ready at the counter.
I'd like to place an order please. Black oil sunflower, forty pounds, and a block of suet. Do you deliver?
Hi Mrs. Marchetti, it's Gary. We deliver in Portland for $6. Black oil is $34 for the forty. Suet blocks are $3.
That's fine. Add a second suet block; one for the woodpeckers and one for me, as I enjoy watching them fight.
Ha. Will do. Delivery tomorrow morning?
Tomorrow morning is fine. I'll leave the side gate unlatched and the check under the flowerpot by the door.
Delivered, left by the back step. The squirrels were already supervising.
Thank you, Gary. I'll deal with the squirrels.
Gary, the cardinal has been at the feeder every day and I'd like to get him some safflower seed. Would that work?
Safflower is exactly right; cardinals love it and squirrels dislike it. Small bag is $11.
Then I'll take one. May I pick it up myself tomorrow morning on my way to the pharmacy?
Sure, we open at 9.
Picked up the safflower, thank you Gary. And please tell your wife the jelly sample was delicious.
Will do. She'll be thrilled.
Spring sale! 10% off all feeders and tomato supports through May 17.
I'd like three tomato cages, the sturdy kind, and a baffle for the pole feeder. The squirrel has learned to leap.
He's a clever one. The dome baffle should do it, $18. Cages are $9 each, sale price $8. I'll bring them by tomorrow afternoon.
Tomorrow afternoon I'm out; leave them by the back step again, please.
Done. Cages and baffle by the back step.
The squirrel has already tried the baffle and slid off like a child on a snow hill. Enormous satisfaction.
Ha! That's the best review we've had.
A hummingbird came to the red feeder this morning. Do I need to change the nectar every few days?
Every three to four days in warm weather. One part sugar to four parts water; no dye, no honey.
Thank you; I'll write that on the index card on the refrigerator.
Bayside Bird & Garden Supply: Your order of thistle seed and suet cakes is ready for pickup.
Thank you. Could someone carry the bags to the car? My back is not what it was.
Absolutely, just pull up by the side door.
Your suet supply is likely getting low. We now have summer suet that doesn't melt in the heat.
Summer suet? I've never heard of it. Do send a few blocks.
Heat-resistant formula. I'll drop them by tomorrow.
Thank you. Put it on my account if you can; I'll pay it with the next order.
No problem.
Left at the back step. One thing, Mrs. Marchetti: finches don't like the old thistle socks once they're moldy; consider a replacement.
Noted; I'll take them down this evening and wash the ports.
I'm told there is a better sort of feeder for chickadees, one with a small perch. Do you stock it?
We do, the cedar one. $18.99. Want us to hold one?
Yes please. I'll come this week.
Held under 'Marchetti'.
Gary, a sparrow family has nested in the wren house. Is there anything I should do?
Leave it be, they'll fledge in a couple of weeks. Don't peek, mama gets nervous.
I'll not peek. I am dreadful at not peeking.
The fledglings are out! Four of them, all squawking on the fence. I couldn't be more proud.
That's great news. Nice work, landlady.
I'd like another forty pounds of black oil; the cardinal is getting through it fast.
Will do. Delivery tomorrow okay?
Tomorrow's fine. The check is under the flowerpot, as always.
Delivered; check collected. Thanks, Mrs. M!
The chickadees took to the new feeder on the first morning. I'm delighted.
Wonderful news! Chickadees are smart. Next, you'll want a heated birdbath for winter.
Don't tempt me; I haven't even got through summer.
Cousin! Bonne année, I'm very late, I know. How is the weather in Portland? We've had a meter of snow.
Bonne année to you too, Eileen. We have had a fair amount ourselves, but nothing like a meter. I hope the roof is holding.
Roof is fine, it's the driveway that's killing my back.
Hire a boy. I did, and he is worth every penny.
Odile, Mama's tourtière recipe, do you have it? Mine never tastes right.
I do, in her handwriting, on a card stained with grease. The secret is a pinch of clove and a little grated apple. Not too much.
APPLE?! I've been doing it wrong for forty years.
You have been doing it wrong in the nicest way.
😂 I'll try it for Easter.
Report back, please.
Joyeuses Pâques in advance. The tourtière was a triumph. Even Marc had seconds, and he hates meat pies.

Splendid. I'll bring lemon bars.
Lemon bars were a hit. Someone asked me if you'd cater their daughter's shower.
I'm seventy-eight. I make lemon bars for friends, not for the public.
I told them you're not for hire. They said pity.
Potluck after the ten o'clock mass next month. Sign-up sheet is in the vestibule. Are you a salad or a dessert?
Dessert. I have a blueberry buckle I've been meaning to make. The berries at the market are good right now.
Wild Maine ones?
Is there any other kind?
Father asked if you'd do the first reading in August. Our regular reader is on vacation.
I'd be honored. I'll practice on the bird feeder.
The chickadees will be a tough crowd.
They're the only ones who don't fidget.
Morning, Odile. Plow didn't make it down Carleton till after seven. I put salt on your front steps while I was at mine.
Walt, you are a gentleman. I'll bring you a loaf of banana bread when I've got the oven going this afternoon.
No need, but I won't say no.
Is Dolores home from the hospital yet? I saw your car come back last evening.
Came home yesterday. Walker and a lot of opinions.
That sounds like Dolores. Tell her the soup is on your porch rail, the chicken one in the blue container.
Found it. She says thank you and that you shouldn't have.
I did, though.
Heads up, street sweeping starts next week. Cars off the street by eight.
Thank you, I'd have forgotten. I'll park the Subaru in the back lane.
Squirrel got into your feeder again. I watched him hanging off it like a circus act.
That's the third one this month. I bought a baffle at Bayside Bird & Garden. Would you mind helping me hang it? It's a two-person job and I don't trust the stepladder.
Sure. Give me ten minutes.
I'll put the kettle on.
Baffle's up. Let's see him get past that.
Marvelous. I shall report back.
Report: he sat on the fence and glared at it for twenty minutes, then gave up.
Good. Nothing beats a defeated squirrel.
Do you still have the long ladder? Mine's got a cracked rung.
It's in the garage behind the lawn chairs. Help yourself, and mind the paint cans.
Will have it back by supper.
Ladder's back. Thanks. Gutters were full of maple seeds.
Walt, a package came for you. It was left on my porch by mistake. A heavy one.
That'll be the tile for the bathroom. Dolores has been waiting on it. I'll come get it.
Take your time. It isn't going anywhere.
Your tomatoes look good over the fence. Mine are a month behind.
I start them on the windowsill in March, and I talk to them. It helps.
I'll try the talking.
Power flickered here around noon. Yours too?
Yes, the stove clock is blinking. I've reset it twice. Casco Light & Power says it should hold now.
Fine by me. I just wanted to know I wasn't alone.
Fireworks in the park again tonight. Dolores wants to know if you'd like to watch from our porch. Better view.
That's kind. I'll see how I feel after supper. I might just stay in with the radio.
Door's open if you change your mind.
Roll call. Who has the cards and who has the good flashlight?
Cards: me. Flashlight: Odile, always. Snacks: Pauline, God help us.
Flashlight and thermos are packed. I've also packed the tide table so nobody wanders out on the rocks at the wrong hour.
She packs a tide table. For a card game.
I'm bringing the scarf I'm not supposed to lose again.
Leaving at nine tomorrow. I'll collect R. at the desk first, signature and all. Pauline, Midge, follow in your car so there's room for her bag and the pillow.
Inn for us, cottage for you. Dock at six for dinner?
Lobster rolls. I've already decided.
Got her. She's in the front seat and has asked three times if we're going to the shore. She is delighted every time.
Checked in. The room smells of lavender, which I assume is the point.
Mine has a fan that sounds like a small airplane.
Come when you're ready. The kettle's on.
Best hand I've held in years and nobody saw it but the ceiling.
R. fell asleep in the chair with her shoes on. Pauline, bring the other blanket in the morning.
On my way at eight with muffins.
Back at the desk by noon. Thank you both. I couldn't have managed the stairs and the bags and her coat and my own nerves.
Nerves nothing, you had a plan.
You always have a plan.
Anyone want a card night at my place this month? Bring your own snacks, I'm out.
I'll bring cheese crackers, the good ones.
I'll bring the cards. Mine are the only deck with every card.
Mine has a missing seven of clubs. I use a bottle cap.
Cheaters play with a bottle cap.
The bottle cap has more integrity than your bidding.
Rude. Accurate. Rude.
Day after tomorrow, then, four o'clock.
Four o'clock. I'll bring the lemon bars too.
Now I'm excited.
Hi Odile! Sandy at Wool & Thistle. The merino you asked about came in this morning, the oatmeal and the dark moss. Shall I hold some for you?
Hello, Sandy. Yes, please hold six skeins of the moss. I'm making a cardigan for myself, since the old one has been mended so often it's more darning than sweater.
Done. They're in a bag with your name on it. Same dye lot, I checked.
Wonderful. I'll come in tomorrow morning, after the pharmacy.
Quick question on the cardigan. The pattern says size 6 needles but my gauge is coming out loose. Should I go down a size?
Go down one size and knit a swatch first. Everyone's tension is different, and yours is an honest tension, so I'd trust the swatch over the pattern.
Swatch done, and you were right. Thank you. I have wasted an evening on stubbornness that you saved me with one sentence.
Happy to help! Reminder that the shop is closed next week for inventory. Back the Monday after.
Thank you for the warning. I'll finish the sleeves by then and won't need anything but buttons.
I just got in some horn buttons, dark brown, a bit like tortoiseshell. Shall I set aside a card of them?
Please do. Those would suit the cardigan well. I'll be in at the end of the week.
Cardigan is blocked and drying on a towel in the spare room. Buttons go on tomorrow. Thank you for everything, Sandy.
Odile, Sandy at Wool & Thistle has the green merino back in. The one you wanted for the cardigan. Better hurry.
Bless you. I'm on my way as soon as I finish this crossword. Did you take any?
Only the dark teal. I left you the moss.
You are a saint. I'll take six skeins of the moss.
I have the moss green. Sandy gave me a ten percent discount for being a loyal customer, which is to say, old.
Take the discount and ask no questions.
I'm on the sleeve and it's twisted. Again. Do you do the ribbing on the long needle or the short?
Short. And for heaven's sake, check that it hasn't twisted before you join the round. Everyone does it once.
Everyone does it once. I've done it four times.
Then you're thorough.
My daughter-in-law is expecting in October. I want to make a blanket but nothing pink or blue.
Cream with a thin gray stripe. Garter stitch, forgiving, and it will wash well. I'll bring you the pattern.
Cream and gray. Perfect.
Knit circle at the library is moving to the community room. The chairs are better.
My back will thank them. Is Marguerite still bringing the shortbread?
She said she would. Don't let her forget.
Joanne, I finished the cardigan body. Only the buttons left. Would you come to Wool & Thistle with me and help me choose? I never trust my own eye.
I'd love to. Bring the swatch.
Those horn buttons were exactly right.
I wore it to the market and a woman stopped me to ask where I'd bought it. I said I'd made it. She didn't believe me.
Flattery.
The blanket is half done and I'm out of cream. Is it too late to match the dye lot?
Call Sandy and give her the number off the ball band. She keeps a ledger.
She keeps a ledger? Of course she does.
Everything good begins with a ledger.
Do you want to do the charity hat drive this fall? The hospital asked for infant caps again.
Count me in. Small and fast, I can do one in an evening.
I'll make a list.
Make it on paper. Phones eat lists.
Ha. Paper it is. I'll bring a clipboard to the circle.
And a pencil with an eraser. We will need it.
Odile! Did you hear they're taking out the card catalog cabinets at Back Cove? Marcy told me at the post office.
I did hear. They asked if I wanted one. I said where on earth would I put it. Then I thought about it for an hour.
Take it! Put your recipes in it.
My recipes live in a shoebox and are perfectly happy.
Fine. But think about the little drawers.
I am thinking about the little drawers. That is the problem.
Lunch next month? The old gang from the staff room. Somewhere with fewer stairs, for my knee.
Fewer stairs, by all means. How about the café on Exchange Street, the one with the ramp?
Perfect. I'll text Barb and Lucille.
Please tell Lucille I'm bringing back her cookbook. Only eleven years late.
She's forgotten she lent it. Don't remind her.
That was fun. Barb hasn't changed one bit. Still correcting the waitress's grammar.
The menu did say "sandwich's." I nearly said something myself.
You wrote it on a napkin. I saw you.
I may have. Old habits.
Crossword question, I'm stuck. Seven letters, "sentinel of the garden," starts with S.
Scarecrow is too long. Is it "sundial"? Seven letters.
Sundial! Of course. You're a treasure.
I did it in ink, so I'm very sure.
My granddaughter's reading test came back and her teacher says she's well above her grade. I nearly cried in the parking lot.
Oh, Carol, that's wonderful. Did you let her pick her own books?
Every week at the library. She comes out with a stack taller than she is.
That's the secret. Let them choose, and then sit still and let them be bored until they read.
What did you do about the mildew on your phlox last year? Mine is white as a sheet.
Baking soda, a little dish soap, and water in a spray bottle. Do it in the morning, never at night.
Writing that down.
Did you see Principal Haskell is retiring? Thirty-something years in education, and they gave him a sheet cake.
I saw the notice in the newsletter. He was a young man when he arrived. All elbows.
They're having a send-off in the gym. Coming?
I'll try. I'd like to see the new library carts, in any case.
I went by Back Cove this morning for the send-off. The gym smelled exactly the same. Floor wax and canned peaches.
Doesn't it? I got teary at the door.
I did not get teary. I got a cinder in my eye.
Of course you did.
They've put the new reading nook where the globe used to stand. I approved.
Plant sale is set for the last weekend of the month. We need two more folding tables from the church hall.
Walt Feeney has a truck. I'll ask him nicely.
I can bring tomato seedlings, about two dozen. Brandywine and a few Sungold.
Odile's tomatoes always sell out first. Please put her at the front table.
Price cards are in the blue bin. Marguerite, would you do the signs?
Happy to. I'll use the big marker this time so nobody squints.
I'll have to leave by one, I'm afraid. I have a standing appointment in the afternoon.
Of course, Odile. You've done more than enough already.
Who has the key to the supply closet? The tape is in there and we're out at the front desk.
I do, but I'm at the dentist until noon.
Odile has a spare, I believe.
I do. It's on the green ribbon in my desk drawer. I'll bring it by this afternoon.
Angel.
Reminder: name tags for the volunteer tea. Bring your own pen.
I'll bring a box of felt-tips. I won't lend them to anyone who doesn't cap them.
She means me.
She means all of us.
Bonjour, ma chère. Still snowing in Montréal. Seventy centimeters in a week, I am not exaggerating.
Bonjour, Margaret. Here it's only slush and Walt next door shoveling like a man possessed. Are you keeping warm?
Soup, and the wool socks you sent at Christmas. They are the only thing between me and the grave.
Dramatic as ever.
I learned from Maman.
She'd be proud. And appalled.
Do you still have Maman's tourtière recipe? Mine comes out dry.
I have it on a card in her handwriting. Pork and a little veal, clove, cinnamon, and do not skimp on the fat. I'll copy it out tonight and put it in the mail.
Mail? Take a photo, Odile.
I'll mail it. Some things deserve a stamp.
You're impossible.
That's what Maman said too.
Luc's wedding is set for the end of September. Saint-Sauveur. You must come.
I'd love to. I'm not certain about the drive, or the border, or my knees, but I'd love to.
Fly to Montréal and I'll collect you at the airport.
Let me think. Tell Luc congratulations from his old cousin.
Old cousin. He'll like that.
Margaret, I looked at the flights. They want a small fortune for an hour in the air. I'm a retired librarian.
Then take the bus. Four hours and a sandwich.
A bus I can manage. Do they have seats with extra legroom?
They have seats. That's the best I can promise.
My hip is being replaced in the fall. The doctor says I'll be dancing by Christmas.
You never danced a day in your life.
Then I'll start. Spite is a good motivator.
I'll send a card with a suitably ridiculous dancing cat.
How is the garden?
The tomatoes are in and the chickadees are fat. The roses have blackspot but I've made my peace with it.
Peace is cheaper than fungicide.
Is the phone call to Canada very dear for you? Mine charges me a fortune for your number.
Mine is included in the plan, strangely. Call whenever you like.
Then I'll call in the evening so we can complain properly.
Margaret, I'll come for the wedding on the bus. I've decided. Book me a room with a bathtub, not a shower. My balance is not what it was.
Wonderful! You'll stay with me. The spare room has a tub the size of a canoe.
That sounds dangerous. I'll take it.
Magnifique. I'll tell Luc.
Good morning, Natalie. I have far too many tomato seedlings again. Would you like four or six for your side of the fence?
Oh, I'd love six, if you can spare them! Are they the same ones as last year? Those were incredible.
The very same. Brandywines, and a few of the little yellow ones. I'll leave them on your porch in the egg cartons.
You're the best. I'll bring you a jar of the rhubarb jam when it's ready.
Natalie, did a package come to your door by mistake? The tracking says delivered, but I can't find it anywhere.
Yes! It was behind my recycling bin. The driver must have been in a hurry. I'll walk it over now.
Thank you, dear. It's only suet cakes for the birds, but the chickadees are very demanding.
Ha! Mine are the same. There's a woodpecker on your feeder right now, by the way. A big one.
That will be the pileated. He comes at about this hour. Don't scare him off, please.
Wouldn't dream of it. Hey, the block party is on for the end of June. Are you in for the lemon bars again?
I suppose I must be. Somebody has to keep the Carleton Street standard up. Put me down for two pans.
Perfect. First tomato on my plant today, green and the size of a walnut. Thought you'd want to know.
Wonderful news. Mine are a week behind, as usual, because I plant too early and then fuss over them. Keep an eye out for hornworms.
Odile, I'm going to be late for the volunteer shift. Parking at the library is a nightmare.
Use the lot behind the courthouse. Free after four, and no one checks.
You are a font of municipal wisdom.
I've been parking in this town since before the lot was paved.
Did you find the donation form I left on the desk?
Yes. I filed it under D, for Donations, and also under J, for Janet, because I don't trust anyone.
Fair.
I also put a lemon bar in the drawer. Don't tell Tom.
My lips are sealed. My mouth is full.
Janet.
Sorry. Delicious.
Odile, are you finished with the book club pick? I'm only on chapter four and the butler is already making me sad.
I finished it a while ago. It gets sadder, but beautifully. Don't skip ahead.
I never skip ahead. Well. Once. In 1989.
You may borrow my copy if the library's is out. It has pencil in the margins.
Pencil I can forgive. Pen would be a scandal.
Odile, it's Louise from the parish. Father Gill asked me to find out who's bringing what to the spring supper. Can I put you down for a dessert?
Of course, Louise. I'll make the apple cake with the cinnamon crumble. It always goes first.
Wonderful. Bless you. We have three people on rolls and nobody on salad yet, so wish me luck.
Ask Marguerite. She makes a very good green salad and she hates being asked for anything harder.
Brilliant. You should run this parish.
Heaven forbid. I'd rather do the crossword.
The supper was a great success. We cleared a good amount for the roof fund. Your cake was gone in ten minutes.
I'm glad to hear it. I left my blue cake plate in the church kitchen. Would you mind keeping it for me until the next time I'm in?
Already in my cupboard with a sticky note on it. Also, the rummage sale is in June. We need people to sort the books. That's your department.
Books are always my department. Send me the hour and I'll bring a pen and a strong opinion about what's worth a quarter.
Nine in the church hall. Wear something you don't mind getting dusty.
Thank you again for sorting all those paperbacks. I found a water-stained Trollope and put it aside for you.
That's very kind. Water-stained is how I like my Trollope. I'll collect it at Mass.
Mrs. Marchetti, Pete Lombardi here. Natalie gave me your number. She says your back porch step is loose?
Good morning, Mr. Lombardi. Yes, the second board from the bottom rocks when I step on it. I would rather fix it than fall on it.
Smart. I can swing by Saturday morning with a few screws and a new tread if it's rotted. Shouldn't take more than an hour.
That would be lovely. I'll have coffee on and pay you for the lumber, of course.
Tread was soft clear through. New one's in, painted gray to match. Lumber was under what I'd spend on lunch, so don't worry about it.
Nonsense, I'll put a check in your mailbox. And thank you for the lovely job. It's very solid now.
Your gutters are full of maple seeds, by the way. Want me to clear them when I'm back with the ladder?
Please do. I'm too old to go up a ladder and too stubborn to admit it to anyone but you.
Ha. I'll come Tuesday afternoon, if the forecast holds.
All clear up there. Found a tennis ball and half a bird's nest. Downspout on the north side is dripping at the joint, so I put a bit of sealant on it.
A tennis ball! The neighbor's dog must be responsible. Thank you again, Mr. Lombardi. There's a jar of tomatoes waiting for you in August.
I'll hold you to it. Call anytime. Pete is fine, by the way.

notes.title: Tourtière
notes.body:
Mother's recipe, the way she did it. Christmas Eve only.

1 lb ground pork
1 lb lean ground beef
1 onion, chopped fine
1 tsp salt
1/2 tsp cloves
1/2 tsp cinnamon
1 potato, boiled and mashed

Simmer the meat with the onion and a little water, about 40 minutes. Stir in the potato at the end. Cool it completely before it goes in the crust, or the bottom goes soggy.

Bake at 400 for 15 minutes, then 350 until the top is golden.

Make two, one to give away. Freezes fine for a month.
